name: Lassalleanism
summary: Lassalleanism is the German socialism of Ferdinand Lassalle (1825-1864). It calls for an independent workers' party that wins universal, equal and direct suffrage by peaceful, lawful agitation, and then uses the state to finance workers' productive associations. These would let workers become their own employers, end profit for outside employers and break the 'iron law' that holds wages near subsistence.
scope: Lassalle's own programme as set out in The Working Man's Programme (1862) and the Open Letter (1863) founding the General German Workers' Association. It excludes later Social Democratic reformism, Marxist critiques of Lassalle, and unsourced stories of dealings with Bismarck.

worker-ownership.rationale: The Open Letter calls for the working class to become "its own employer" in large productive associations, so that the whole product of labour goes to the workers; Kirkup reads the goal as a collectivism.

state-finances-worker-businesses.rationale: Lassalle holds that workers cannot raise the capital for productive associations themselves and that the only road to emancipation is free labour associations through "the helping hand of the State".

profit-exploitation.rationale: The Open Letter says the wage is only what barely supports life while the surplus of the enterprise falls to the employing class, and proposes abolishing the profit of enterprise.

wages-fall-to-bare-minimum.rationale: The Open Letter states the "iron and cruel law" that wages are held at barely enough to support life, and treats it as the rule of the existing wage system.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: In the associations the Open Letter has the wage disappear and be replaced by the full reward of labour, the goal of the working-class movement.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Open Letter wants the whole production of labour to be the claim of the worker, with no profit going to an outside employer.

workers-own-party.rationale: The Open Letter says the working class must constitute itself as an independent political party, separate from the Progressive Party.

property-franchise.rationale: The Programme attacks the property census as the mark of bourgeois rule, and the Open Letter makes universal, equal and direct suffrage the workers' core demand.

racial-franchise.rationale: A franchise limited to one group contradicts the universal and equal suffrage Lassalle demands for all as men; he never discusses race.

direct-action.rationale: The Open Letter says the workers' political programme is peaceful and lawful agitation for representation in the legislatures, not action outside them.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Lassalle urges "peaceful and lawful agitation with all lawful means" while describing the Prussian government as a disguised absolutism.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: His whole route is suffrage, workers' representatives in the legislature, then state help for the associations that end the wage system.

refuse-to-join-illegitimate-government.rationale: He faults the Progressives for carrying on parliamentary business with a government they had declared unconstitutional, and says they should close the sessions instead.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The Programme shows each ruling class loading the costs of the state onto others and writing its privilege into law, but holds the true nature of the state to be a moral whole.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Programme makes the working-class principle the claim of all, as men, to share in directing the will of the state.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Programme says any person may claim a share in the state as a man and a reasonable being, without property, and the Open Letter demands equal suffrage.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Programme describes bourgeois wealth being turned into a legal condition of political power, as the privilege of landed nobles had been.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: The Programme condemns indirect taxes on salt, corn, beer and fuel because the poorest pay nearly all of them, but sets out no specific demand to cut them.

taxation-theft.rationale: The Programme treats taxation as the proper way to bear the costs of the state and objects only to privileged classes shifting them onto the propertyless.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Programme says the right to property lawfully earned is legitimate and unassailable, and objects only when wealth becomes a condition of political power.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Programme holds it the state's duty to help the working poor to a fuller wage and education, as its true aim.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Workers who become their own employers in large associations run their enterprises themselves, as the Open Letter describes.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The Programme calls the growth of industry and capital in bourgeois hands the revolutionary force of the early modern period, bringing vast wealth.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Lassalle treats factory production and division of labour as the real revolutionary force and wants workers to take over large factories, not abandon them.

revolution-justified.rationale: Lassalle calls revolution, legal or violent, certain to come, and admits to being a revolutionary, yet the Programme says one cannot be made and his own programme is lawful agitation.

political-violence-never.rationale: He says revolution will come either lawfully or as a violent whirlwind, and he praises armed resolve in the French bourgeoisie, so he does not rule violence out.

class-collaboration.rationale: He calls the workers' cause a cry of union against privilege and "of love", yet splits the workers from the Progressives and aims to end the employing class's profit.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: He explains 1789 and the failure of German liberalism by material interests, and says revolutions enter real relations before they win recognition, though he also treats history as the growth of freedom.

class-struggle-history.rationale: He reads French history since 1789 and German history since 1848 as outcomes of which class interest stands behind a demand, though he does not call class conflict the sole engine.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Lassalle wants the state won by suffrage and used for labour associations, but also wants the army and officials remodelled so that they can never oppose the people.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: He says the Diet's right to grant the budget is a constitutional right and bars any compromise on it, calling a Diet that yields the government's accomplice.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Lassalle coins and mocks the "night-watchman" state limited to protecting person and property, and says a state led by the workers' idea would take on a moral mission.

state-harmful.rationale: He calls the state the means by which humanity wins freedom from want and ignorance and the helper of labour, and mocks views that would make it dispensable.

positive-liberty.rationale: He says free activity of the individual alone is not enough when people are unequal in strength and wealth, and adds a solidarity of interests and common development, with the state's help.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: He shows caution money and stamp duty making the press a preserve of capital, and attacks papers that put the publishers' capital above the truth.

decide-locally.rationale: He holds that sovereignty is indivisible and that German unity needs the thirty-four separate sovereignties merged into one, calling federalism impotent.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: He calls a central power sharing authority with separate state sovereignties a contradiction and federalism impotent.

head-commands-forces.rationale: He wants the army remodelled so that it can never be the monarch's instrument against the people, with officers elected by the troops and civil courts over it.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: He attacks absolutism and pseudo-constitutionalism, and wants constitutional rights held against a government that tramples them.

simple-living.rationale: He tells workers frugality in needs is a misfortune and the virtue of the age is to have as many needs as possible and meet them honestly.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: He praises a growing range of needs as the spur of a people's culture, though he says nothing on status goods as such.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: He traces the wages that hold workers near subsistence to the wage system and proposes an institutional cure, associations through the state.

notes: Sources read: the full Programme and Open Letter (English pamphlet, checked against the German transcription), the GHDI excerpt and the speech excerpts in Voices of Revolt (1927 translation, from the Marxists Internet Archive). Searched themes (also Kirkup's 1913 History of Socialism, ch. V): economy (associations, wages, taxes, property, trade unions, tariffs, public ownership), government (suffrage, parliament, budget, monarchy, courts, federalism), liberty (press, assembly, state limits), society (family, gender, religion), world (nation, war, alliances), culture, ecology and technology. Lassalle's surviving defining texts say nothing on most of these, so they stay null; the FES history PDF is robots-blocked and Marx, Luxemburg and Kautsky are critics, not used. The statement-pass candidates for state finance and the subsistence wage law (state-finances-worker-businesses, wages-fall-to-bare-minimum) are answered here.
